title: Cost-optimal Seeding Strategy During a Botanical Pandemic in Domesticated Fields
short_title: Cost-optimal seeding strategy during a botanical pandemic
abstract: Botanical pandemics cause enormous economic damage and food shortages around the globe. However, since botanical pandemics are here to stay in the short-medium term, domesticated field owners can strategically seed their fields to optimize each session’s economic profit. In this work, we propose a novel epidemiological-economic mathematical model that describes the economic profit from a field of plants during a botanical pandemic. We describe the epidemiological dynamics using a spatiotemporal extended susceptible-infected-recovered epidemiological model with a non-linear output economic model. We provide an algorithm to obtain an optimal grid-formed seeding strategy to maximize economic profit, given field and pathogen properties. We show that the recovery and basic infection rates have a similar economic influence. Unintuitively, we show that a larger farm does not promise higher economic profit. Our results demonstrate a significant benefit of using the proposed seeding strategy and shed more light on the dynamics of the botanical pandemic.
summary: Plant disease pandemics cause enormous economic damage and food shortages, and they are here to stay in the short to medium term. We built a mathematical model linking the spread of a plant disease across a field to the field's economic profit, along with an algorithm that finds the grid-shaped seeding pattern that maximizes profit for given field and pathogen properties. We found that recovery and infection rates have a similar economic influence, and that a larger farm does not promise higher profit.
key_findings: We combined a spatiotemporal extended susceptible-infected-recovered epidemic model with a non-linear economic output model for a field of plants.
We provide an algorithm that finds an optimal grid-formed seeding strategy to maximize profit, given field and pathogen properties.
The recovery rate and the basic infection rate have a similar economic influence.
